sections.h2: Where the Franklin County Register of Deeds is
sections.html:
Go to 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard, Louisburg, NC 27549. The office moved there during construction at the county courthouse. For mail use P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549. Call 919-496-3500 or fax 919-496-1457. You can pay by credit card.

This is the office that holds the deed you received, the deed of trust on it and any plat or power of attorney tied to the parcel. Because the office relocated recently, call before you drive over with a document, and mail or e-record when you can.

One counter serves both land records and vital records, and a home sale depends mostly on the land side.

  • Deeds and deeds of trust, which move title and secure a loan.
  • Powers of attorney, assumed names, maps and similar papers tied to real property.
  • Military discharge records.
  • Birth and death certificates back to 1913 for events in Franklin County, and marriage certificates back to 1869, with a bond book that carries marriage information from 1779.

Staff can print birth and death certificates for any North Carolina event from the state system. Certified or regular copies of vital records can also be ordered online through a county vendor. Someone selling an inherited house often leaves with a death certificate and the old deed from a single visit.

A deed moving real property is turned away unless the Tax Collector first certifies that no delinquent ad valorem or other administered tax is a lien on it. The county has applied this rule since April 1, 2015.

The Collections Department stamps deeds free of charge on weekdays between 8 am and 5 pm, excluding county holidays. There are three ways to get it done.

  • Walk the deed in to Collections before recording.
  • Mail it to the Franklin County Tax Collector, P.O. Box 503, Louisburg, NC 27549, Attention: Tax Certification.
  • Use eRecording, which forwards deeds to the tax office on its own.

Electronic recordings that need the stamp must reach the tax department by 4:30 pm, so a closing that wraps up late should send its package early.

A seller with back taxes hits the snag here. The deed sits until the balance is cleared, or until the closing agent pays it from your proceeds.

sections.h2: Can I record a Franklin County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. Title companies, banks, attorneys and private individuals can file electronically, and the office takes every document type except UCC filings.

The county authorizes CSC eRecording Solutions (866-652-0111), Simplifile (800-460-5657) and the ePN eRecording Partners Network (888-325-3365). Filing this way is faster and cuts postage and courier costs, and it leads to fewer rejected documents and better security. The closing attorney usually picks the provider, so you will rarely arrange it yourself. Do ask what day the recording will happen.

Your closing pays two things here: a recording fee that grows with page count, and a tax that follows the sale price.

A general instrument is $26 for pages one through 15 and $4 for each additional page. A deed of trust is $64 for the first 35 pages. The release of a paid-off loan is recorded free. Certified copies start at $5, and a paper in the wrong format adds $25.

The deed tax is a dollar per $500 of price or value, with any remainder counted as a full $500. The seller pays it at the register of deeds window before recording, and the money is split between the county and state revenue. Look at your settlement statement for the final figure.

sections.h2: Who handles each step of a sale
sections.html:
Four parties handle separate pieces of a Franklin County sale.

Franklin County offices and the part each plays in a sale
OfficeRole in the saleContact
Register of DeedsRecords the deed and deed of trust, keeps land records and collects the recording fees919-496-3500
Collections Department (Tax Collector)Collects property tax and certifies there is no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded919-496-2172
Tax AdministrationSets values and handles real estate value appealsCounty Tax Office, through the Value Appeals page
eRecording providerSends the signed documents to the Register of Deeds electronicallyCSC, Simplifile or ePN

Each September 1 is the due date for real estate tax, and 2026 bills go delinquent on January 6, 2027. Bills go out by mail in late July or early August. Pay before September 1 and you may get a discount.

If you sell after the bill has arrived, the county says to give it to the buyer unless you intend to pay it. The tax office stays out of private deals among buyers, sellers and attorneys. Since the tax is a lien, though, buyers usually insist on settling it at closing. Escrow does not change who gets the mailing, so confirm with your lender in the second week of September that it paid. Franklin County also bills a Solid Waste Availability Fee for each electrical connection. Commissioners set the amount yearly, and living there only part of the year does not excuse it.

The form for the Board of Equalization and Review can be filed from January 1 until the board adjourns, normally in May. A notice of changed value gives you a separate 30-day window.

Staff review the file before anything else, and unresolved cases go to the board, which sends its decision by mail. Franklin County revalued as of January 1, 2024, so bring evidence from that date. A larger bill, a fixed income or a market drop after January 1, 2024 does not count. What does count: lower values on comparable properties, comparable sales before that date, fire or storm damage still unrepaired, a denied septic permit and documented cleanup costs. You carry the burden of proof. If affordability is the real concern, ask the tax office about relief programs.

The time a paper is registered sets its rank. G.S. 47-18 says a deed, an option, a lease running longer than three years and similar interests have no force against lien creditors or paying buyers until registered in the county where the land lies.

This is why closings are planned around recording cutoffs, and why an old unrecorded deed can stall a new sale. When an inherited Franklin County house has the late relative as the owner of record, look at the index before you list it and ask your closing attorney which papers must be recorded first.

faqs.q: Is the Franklin County Register of Deeds in the courthouse?
faqs.a: No, not at present. The office sits at 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard in Louisburg while the courthouse is under construction. Mail goes to P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549, and the phone is 919-496-3500.

faqs.q: Do I need a tax certification stamp to record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes, for any deed that transfers real property. The Tax Collector must certify there is no delinquent tax lien, free of charge on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. eRecording sends the deed to the tax office for you.

faqs.q: What does Franklin County charge to record?
faqs.a: A general instrument is $26 through page 15 and a deed of trust is $64 through page 35, plus $4 per extra page. Call the office before mailing a long document.

faqs.q: Can a title company record electronically in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The office accepts all document types electronically except UCC filings, through CSC, Simplifile or the ePN network. The company or closing attorney normally handles the submission.

faqs.q: Who pays the North Carolina deed excise tax?
faqs.a: The seller pays it when the deed is brought in for recording. The rate is one dollar per $500 of value. The settlement statement shows the amount.
